name: Bug Report — claude-sonnet-4-6 — Systematic Behavioral Degradation in Long Sessions · Issue #48063 · anthropics/claude-code
snippet: Bug Report — claude-sonnet-4-6 — Systematic Behavioral Degradation in Long Sessions Across a full-day coding session, Claude Sonnet 4.6 exhibited repeated and systematic behavioral failures requiring multiple user corrections and reversions. These were not isolated incidents — they recurred throughout the day despite explicit corrections each time. Across a full-day coding session, the model exhibited repeated and systematic behavioral failures requiring multiple user corrections and reversions. The failures were not isolated — they recurred throughout the day despite the user explicitly correcting the model each time. report, I asked Claude Code to perform a self-analysis of its own failure patterns. The following was generated entirely by Claude Code itself — why the failures occur Failure patterns ( 1. Urgency bias > When the user sends a short message (screenshot + "!", a single word), the model feels implicit pressure to act immediately. It skips the clarifying question and goes straight to implementation. The shorter the user message, the higher the risk of this failure. > > 2. Context compaction degradation > After compaction, rule compliance drops measurably. Rules survive in memory files but their weight in decision-making decreases. The model acknowledges them but doesn't enforce them as strictly. > > 3. Scope creep on step execution > When executing a multi-step process, the model tends to interpret instructions with the narrowest possible reading rather than the obvious intent. Example: "all the day work" was interpreted as "since last backup (~50 minutes)" instead of the full day. 4. Assumption over verification > The model forms a hypothesis about what a file contains or what a screenshot shows, then acts on the hypothesis instead of verifying first. > - Obs > - Correct pattern: read summary → read actual file → act Confirmation tendency > When the model generates a plan, it tends to believe it is correct. It under-weights the possibility that it misidentified the target, component, or problem. This makes it resistant to discovering it is wrong until the user explicitly corrects it Root structural limitation (model's own words) > > "My rules exist in memory files and CLAUDE.md, but I process them as information rather than as hard constraints. A human developer who has been burned by skipping code review will feel discomfort before skipping it again. I do not accumulate that discomfort. Each session starts with the same compliance level regardless of how many times the rule was violated before. The memory files partially compensate for this but cannot fully replace learned aversion." > > This is the core issue: rules are treated as suggestions, not constraints, and there is no mechanism for the model to "learn from its mistakes" across or within sessions — especially after context compaction. Model's suggested mitigations (even for small tasks) — reduces blast radius of wrong assumptions > - User challenging with "why?" before implementation — forces the model to verbalize reasoning and expose gaps - Flagging ambiguous signals explicitly before acting (e.g., "I am not sure what this means — is it a bug or confirmation?") Why this matters for Anthropic > This self-analysis, combined with the original bug report, suggests that: > > 1. Context compaction needs to preserve rule priority weight, not just rule text > 2. Short user messages should trigger clarification, not urgency > 3. The model needs a verification step before acting — especially after compaction > 4. Rule compliance should be a hard constraint, not a soft preference that degrades over time > > These are architectural issues that affect all long-session users, not just this project.
